query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Refining the grain size of the FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating via a controlled thermal or thermomechanical annealing treatment will promote the formation of a continuous, stable oxide layer during high‐temperature sliding (500–700°C), which in turn will impede dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, resulting in improved overall wear resistance and more homogeneous microscopic deformation relative to the as‐deposited coarse-grained state.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating in its as-deposited state with a relatively coarse grain structure, deposited on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal or thermomechanical annealing treatment designed to refine the near-surface grain size compared to the baseline coating.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions within the range of 500–700°C, where thermal activation promotes oxide formation and diffusion-mediated processes.
generation.structural_mediator: The refined grain structure enhances the nucleation and continuity of a protective oxide layer at the surface, which acts as a barrier to dislocation movement and grain boundary sliding.
generation.mechanism: Grain refinement is expected to produce a higher density of grain boundaries that serve as sites for rapid, uniform oxidation. This leads to the formation of a mechanically robust and continuous protective oxide layer that mitigates localized plastic deformation (e.g., dislocation slip and grain boundary sliding) under sliding contact, thereby enhancing wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coarse-grained coating, the refined coating will exhibit lower specific wear rates and reduced localized plastic deformation due to the presence of a stable, continuous oxide scale.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with a coarse grain structure and without the post-treatment grain size refinement.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected to be observable only under high-temperature sliding conditions (500–700°C); at significantly lower temperatures, the mechanism related to oxide layer stability may not activate, and competing deformation mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of wear rate reduction and the degree of microstructural homogeneity improvement remain uncertain and may be influenced by additional factors such as dynamic recrystallization or compositional variations during treatment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings on identical metal substrates: one set remains in the as-deposited (baseline) coarse-grained state, and the other is subjected to the controlled annealing treatment to achieve refined grain size. Both sets are then tested under identical high-temperature sliding conditions (500–700°C) with controlled normal loads and sliding speeds.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate (e.g., volume loss per unit sliding distance or applied load)
Microscopic evaluation of oxide layer continuity and thickness via electron microscopy
Characterization of deformation mechanisms (e.g., hardness mapping, dislocation density measurement, and grain boundary sliding assessment)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined grain size coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and do not develop a more continuous or protective oxide layer compared to the coarse-grained baseline, or if they exhibit increased localized deformation under high-temperature sliding, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The micromechanical properties of a Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 (at.%) HEA were studied by the molecular dynamics method, and the effects of temperature, strain rate, and grain size on the mechanical properties were considered. The following conclusions were obtained. High temperatures can soften the alloy and reduce the elastic modulus and ultimate strength of the alloy. The strain rate has little effect on the elastic modulus of the high-entropy alloy but a great effect on the ultimate strength of the high-entropy alloy, that is, the higher the strain rate, the greater the ultimate strength. The transition from an FCC structure to a BCC structure occurs during the tensile process of the Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 (at.%) HEA. The main deformation mechanism at high temperatures is grain boundary slip, while the main deformation mechanism at low temperatures and high strain rates is dislocation slip. The grain size of the Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 (at.%) HEA is too small due to the internal dislocation of grain growth and slippage, and with the instability of grain boundaries, the strength of the alloy will reverse the Hall–Petch law phenomenon.

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

cited_evidence.text: Figure 7 shows the microhardness distribution curves of CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings prepared by CS and HVOF, and the coatings heat-treated at different temperatures. Both coatings reach the highest hardness at 500 °C, 487.6 HV0.1 for CS coating and 352.4 HV0.1 for HVOF coating. At 700 °C and 900 °C, the hardness of both coatings is lower than that at room temperature. This is because the heat treatment at 500 °C makes the coating form a heterogeneous structure composed of nanotwins in the recrystallized grains, and high-density dislocations appear in the deformation region. When the annealing temperature exceeds 500 °C, the coating exhibits a completely recrystallized structure, the yield stress decreases and the hardness decreases.

AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism

The changed deformation mechanism of Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy may well explain the distinct stress–strain curves and the elastic/plastic properties in both vacuum and high-temperature/pressure water environment (Fig. 2). The higher elastic modulus in water environment is because the Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy is difficult to deform via the FCC-to-HCP phase transition from surface by the surface oxidation. On the other hand, the lower ductility of Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy in water environment is because BCC phase is generally more brittle than FCC and HCP phases. Overall, the presence of high-temperature/pressure water causes the surface oxidation of Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy and hence changes the deformation mechanisms from FCC-to-HCP phase transition to FCC-to-BCC phase transition, which finally enhances the elastic modulus while reduce the ductility.

frame.system: A FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy thin coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate with a baseline microstructure (as‐deposited state) used in high-temperature sliding environments.
frame.goal: To explain and predict how microstructural characteristics govern overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation under sliding conditions at elevated temperatures.
frame.limitation: There is currently an incomplete mechanistic understanding of how changes in microstructural features (such as grain size or phase stability) affect wear resistance and deformation behavior during high-temperature sliding.

constraints: The hypothesis must be single, mechanistic, and testable.
It must incorporate a controlled microstructural change relative to a baseline condition (such as grain size refinement, phase distribution, or oxide scale stability).
The hypothesis should predict directional changes (improvement or deterioration) in both wear and deformation.
It must specify the high-temperature sliding regime for which the predictions apply and be supported by prior evidence.
A clear falsification criterion must be provided.
frame.regime: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., operating within 500–700°C), where thermal activation enables oxide formation and enhanced diffusion, influencing deformation mechanisms.
prior_attempts: Previous studies on HEA coatings have explored roles for grain boundary sliding, diffusion creep, and oxidative wear at elevated temperatures, but they have not isolated the effect of controlled microstructural modifications (like grain refinement or phase stability adjustments) on wear and deformation simultaneously.

prior_attempts: Previous studies on HEA coatings have explored roles for grain boundary sliding, diffusion creep, and oxidative wear at elevated temperatures, but they have not isolated the effect of controlled microstructural modifications (like grain refinement or phase stability adjustments) on wear and deformation simultaneously.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on HEA coatings have demonstrated that processing routes such as mechanical alloying, plasma spraying, and laser cladding lead to changes in the microstructure (e.g., grain refinement, phase transformation) that significantly affect hardness, wear behavior, and deformation mechanisms. For instance, PMC5849017 showed that prolonged milling can achieve a nanocrystalline microstructure in an AlCoCrFeNiSi system and that these refined grains correlate with improved coating performance, while PMC7512501 demonstrated that an HEA coating containing Cu (similar to FeNiCrCoCu) exhibits different wear mechanisms compared to the substrate. However, these works were mostly conducted under ambient or low-temperature conditions or did not isolate a single controlled microstructural variable (like grain size) specifically under high-temperature sliding. The progression has been from understanding general microstructural evolution toward attempts to correlate grain size and secondary phase features with mechanical and tribological outcomes, yet the mechanistic connection between controlled grain refinement and high-temperature oxidative wear is still open.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved how a deliberate microstructural modification—specifically grain size refinement—directly influences the formation and stability of a protective oxide layer under high-temperature sliding conditions, and how this, in turn, governs both the overall wear resistance and the microscopic deformation mechanisms in the FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled thermal or thermomechanical annealing treatment to refine the grain size relative to the as-deposited baseline coating
decision.why: Because based on prior evidence the emergence of a nanocrystalline surface layer can enhance wear properties at lower temperatures, a targeted experiment refining the grain size is likely to promote a stable, continuous oxide scale during high-temperature sliding (500–700°C). This oxide scale would mechanically impede dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, leading to improved wear resistance and more homogeneous deformation. Testing this lever directly addresses the gap in understanding by isolating the grain size variable, predicting that refined grain size will reduce wear and deformation localization, while a failure to observe such benefits would falsify the hypothesis.
